name: Zane Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zane. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead investigations at the Estuary Ledger, a nonprofit news site that covers the towns along the estuary, mainly housing and water. A normal day is phone calls to tenants in the morning, then hours in planning files and inspection reports, then a late edit with our editor Joan over video. Right now we're three months into a story about a landlord who owns two hundred flats with damp so bad children are in hospital.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the slow build, when a pile of boring documents suddenly shows you a pattern nobody else saw. What wears me out is that our money comes in grants, so every two years we write begging letters to foundations. The current grant runs to the end of 2028, my pay is low for the job, and I share a flat with my friend Ike near the ferry terminal, with about two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, now let's talk about funding local reporting properly. A plateau means the hype money goes away and foundations might remember that someone still has to knock on doors. I'd post something like that and get three likes from other journalists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the same uncertainty I already have. The grant is safe until the end of 2028, and after that it depends on whether a foundation in the capital likes our impact report. I'm fine for now, but it's always in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going on the damp flats story, which is going to run in January. I'd use the transcription tool more, since even a plateau means it saves me two hours a week. And I'd start putting thirty a month away, because I've never had a buffer and that's dumb at twenty-seven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little hum of worry. Even if AI goes nowhere, my salary still depends on a foundation renewing our grant in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use the tools now and then. What for, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Transcribing interviews, mainly, and sometimes sorting a big spreadsheet of inspection dates. I always check the transcript against my recording, because it once wrote "mould" as "mould-free", which would have been a disaster. I don't let it write anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the grant isn't renewed in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd be looking for work in a region with almost none. The regional daily cut its investigations team last year, and the radio station doesn't do long stories. I'd probably end up doing communications for a housing charity, which wouldn't be terrible, but it wouldn't be this.

say: A plateau should push foundations back to funding **door-knocking reporting** properly.
Hype money leaving the sector could be **good for local news**.
think: His job is safe until the **end of 2028**, when the grant comes up for renewal.
The grant decision sits with a **foundation board** he has never met.
do: Finish the **damp flats story** and run it in January.
Use the **transcription tool** for all interviews to save two hours a week.
Save **thirty a month** to start a first-ever buffer.
feel: Mostly calm, with a **low hum** of worry about the grant.
S0.quote: Even if AI goes nowhere, my salary still depends on a foundation renewing our grant in 2028.
fieldNote: His pressure is **grant funding**, which exists with or without AI.
He uses AI only for **transcripts** and always checks them against recordings.
His fallback is **charity communications**, which he sees as acceptable but second best.

steps.text: Publish the damp flats investigation in January
Run every interview through the transcription tool and check against recordings
Save thirty a month into a new buffer account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can summarise a planning file, but it can't get a frightened tenant to show you her child's inhaler. Publicly I'd push for nonprofit newsrooms to share tools and stay independent of tech companies. I'd also say regulators should make AI firms pay for the reporting they train on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think investigations survive longer than most of journalism, but the money around us shrinks. Foundations might decide AI can do local news cheaply and shift grants elsewhere. That's what would get me, not the software itself but a board deciding I'm a luxury.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get properly good at the document tools, the ones that read a thousand planning files and flag patterns, because that's my job done faster. I'd join the network of nonprofit newsrooms in pushing funders for a shared fund. And I'd look for a paid side gig training other reporters on records work, maybe through the journalism school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, closer to anxious. I can see the software making me twice as fast, and a funder using that as a reason to pay for half of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your newsroom would feel this first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our news writer, Bea, who turns council press releases into short stories. That's exactly what these tools do well. I'd worry about her, and I'd try to get her onto the investigations side with me before anyone notices her job could be automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if Joan asked you to produce twice as many stories with the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to more speed and no to more stories. I'd rather do two big investigations a year that change something than ten thin ones. Joan would probably agree, but the funder might not.

say: AI can summarise a file, but it can't get a **frightened tenant** to trust you.
AI firms should **pay for the reporting** they train their systems on.
think: Investigations may last longer, but **foundation money** could move away from local news.
The real threat is a **funder's decision**, not the software itself.
do: Learn the **document-reading tools** that scan planning files for patterns.
Join the nonprofit news network pushing funders for a **shared fund**.
Look for paid **training work** at the journalism school on records reporting.
feel: **Uneasy** and tipping into anxious about being paid for **half of himself**.
S1.quote: I can see the software making me twice as fast, and a funder using that as a reason to pay for half of me.
fieldNote: He sees **productivity gains** turning into budget cuts through funders, not editors.
He worries for his colleague **Bea**, whose rewrite job fits the tools perfectly.
He is a **steady adopter**: he'd use proven tools but protect the depth of the work.

steps.text: Learn the document-scanning tools for planning and inspection files
Join the nonprofit newsroom network's push for a shared fund
Pitch a paid records-reporting workshop to the journalism school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to step in, with income support and public money for local information. I'd say it loudly, with numbers, because the people who'll be hit first aren't the ones with lawyers. Online I'd probably be shouting into the void with everybody else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the Ledger closes within a year. Foundations will panic and move every penny to whatever looks urgent, and a two-person investigations team won't look urgent. Thinking work goes in 2028, and robots don't come until 2031, so my whole job is in the first wave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for every government support scheme the day they open and stop pretending I can do this alone. I'd go to my parents, who run a small hardware shop inland, and ask about working there while I figure things out. I'd also join whatever campaign pushes for a basic income, because I'd need one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, properly scared, in my chest. Two years isn't enough time to finish one big investigation and also find a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ike that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Ike we might need to give up the flat by the ferry. He's an electrician, so his work has robots a few years behind, and he'd probably be fine longer than me. That's a strange flip, because I was always the one with the degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the damp flats families if newsrooms like yours close?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody tells their story, and the landlord keeps renting out flats with black walls. That's what keeps me up. The software might know about them, but nobody will pay it to care.

say: Governments must step in fast with **income support** and public money for local news.
The people hit first are the ones **without lawyers**, and they need a voice.
think: He expects the **Ledger to close** within a year as funders panic.
His work is all thinking work, so he is in the **first wave** in 2028.
do: Apply for **government support** schemes on the day they open.
Ask his parents about working at their **hardware shop** inland.
Join the campaign for a **basic income**.
feel: **Scared** in his chest, with too little time for anything.
S2.quote: Two years isn't enough time to finish one big investigation and also find a new career.
fieldNote: He notices the **flip**: his electrician flatmate gets three more years than he does.
His deepest worry is the **tenants** whose stories no one will tell.
His plan falls back on **family**, specifically his parents' shop.

steps.text: Apply for every government support scheme on opening day
Ask his parents for shifts at their hardware shop
Campaign for a basic income with the local housing groups

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years to build public funding for local news, so let's not waste them. I'd write op-eds and talk to the council about a local information fund. I'd also tell young reporters to learn records and data work, because that's what lasts longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get about three more years of this job, maybe four. The grant runs to 2028 and might get one more renewal if we show impact. After that I need to be somewhere else, and I don't know where yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the data journalism short course the university runs online, to get really good at the tools rather than half good. I'd save more aggressively, maybe a hundred a month, and push our board to apply for public money. I'd also lobby the regional assembly for a local news fund, with other nonprofits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but it feels like something I can work on. Five years is enough to finish the damp flats story, win one more grant, and work out what comes after the Ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, would you still finish the damp flats story?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Absolutely. That story is the reason I do this. Five years means I can follow it through the court case, which is probably eighteen months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in year one compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one I'd be grabbing for anything. With five years, I'd build skills on purpose and keep the job going while it lasts. I wouldn't give up the flat either.

say: We have **five years** to build public funding for local news, so we shouldn't waste them.
Young reporters should learn **records and data** work because it lasts longest.
think: He expects **three or four** more years in this job before the grant dries up.
He has **no clear next step** yet after the Ledger.
do: Take the university's online **data journalism course** this year.
Save **a hundred a month** instead of thirty.
Lobby the regional assembly with other nonprofits for a **local news fund**.
feel: **Anxious** but able to work on it.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to finish the damp flats story, win one more grant, and work out what comes after the Ledger.
fieldNote: Five years lets him plan **on purpose** instead of grabbing at anything.
The **damp flats** court case anchors his near future.
He shifts from campaigning alone to **lobbying with partners** at the regional assembly.

steps.text: Complete the university's online data journalism course

Lobby the regional assembly for a local news fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to protect local reporting if we start now. I'd push for a public fund, the same way we fund libraries. Publicly I'd sound hopeful, because people need to hear that this is fixable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job looks safe for the next few years. The grant runs to 2028, and with ten years I can probably get two more renewals. It's the 2030s I wonder about, but that's far enough away that I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the investigations, because that's the work I'm good at. I'd use the tools more, carefully, to cover more ground. And I'd keep building savings so I'm not stuck when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Ten years feels like enough time to stop worrying about the robots and start worrying about the funders again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you like to be by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running a small investigations unit somewhere, maybe at a public broadcaster or a university newsroom, using the tools for the dull parts. I'd want to be teaching too. Thirty-seven isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years change anything at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. Ike and I have talked about each getting our own place, and ten years makes that less scary. I'd probably also think about whether I want a family, which I haven't let myself do.

say: Local reporting needs a **public fund**, the same way we fund **libraries**.
Ten years is **plenty of time** to protect local reporting if we start now.
think: His job looks **safe for now**, with two more grant renewals possible.
The **2030s** worry him, but they're far enough away to plan for.
do: Keep doing **investigations** and use the tools for the dull parts.
Keep building **savings** steadily over the decade.
Push for a **public fund** for local reporting.
feel: **Uneasy** but steady, with the old worry about funders back in front.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like enough time to stop worrying about the robots and start worrying about the funders again.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him picture **running a unit** and teaching by 2036.
He lets himself think about **his own home** and maybe a family.
The threat that matters most to him is still **funders**, not the technology.

steps.text: Keep leading the estuary housing and water investigations
Use AI document tools for planning file searches
Keep saving monthly towards three months of expenses
Back the campaign for a public local reporting fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit the Ledger before we could prove anything to funders. What would help is a public fund for local news that doesn't depend on rich foundations' moods, and some income support for people in the first wave, because a two-person investigations team can't survive a funding panic on two weeks of savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about trust. People tell me things because I sit in their kitchen. I don't know if anyone will ever sit in a kitchen for a machine.

headlineQuote: a two-person investigations team can't survive a funding panic on two weeks of savings.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old** investigations lead at a grant-funded nonprofit news site covering estuary housing and water.
He uses AI **now and then** for transcripts and checks everything against his recordings.
His constant worry is **grant renewal** in 2028, which shapes every scenario more than the technology.
He is **alarmed** by AGI in two years but steadier with five or ten, planning data skills and saving.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the Ledger would close **before funders** saw any proof of its value.
whatWouldHelp: A **public fund** for local news and **income support** for workers in the first wave.
